context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the TREP Wire podcast, the show where commercial real estate needs data and insights. This is our week in review for the week ending September 4th, 2026. I'm Haley Keen with TREP, a data modeling and analytics firm for the CMBS, commercial real estate and CLO markets. I'm with Lonnie Hendry, chief product officer, and Stephen Bushbaum, head of applied research and analytics. Last week, we discussed what Kevin Warsh might say during his first Jackson Hole address as Fed Chair. He delivered a firmly hawkish message, and markets responded by sharply increasing the odds of a September rate hike. Since then, oil prices and global bond yields have climbed, while the latest employment data have pointed to slower hiring. That leaves investors weighing softer labor conditions against persistent inflation risks. On today's episode, we'll also dig into student housing as college football returns, including a $435 million portfolio acquisition, before carrying that same theme into some of our property-type stories. Capital is still moving across commercial real estate, but only for the right assets, markets, and business plans. So, Stephen, let's start at the top here. Are higher rates shutting down capital or simply making it much more selective? I think selective is exactly the right word. The bond market is repricing risk, but the series stories this week suggest that capital markets have not simply closed. I think all dealmakers know this at this point. I mean, higher rates have not shut down things. They've just had us sharpen our pencils and recalibrate. So we have some really interesting stories this week. We have a $340 million Chicago office refinancing supported by recent leasing momentum and nearly $500 million of acquisition financing for an industrial portfolio. So clearly big deals still getting done, able to be underwritten at, well, fairly higher rates. I mean, the 10-year yield has pushed up to, gosh, we're touching 4.8% recently, and it looks like 5% is yet again within reach. At the same time, we had an office loan that already received an extension, but it's back in special servicing. We have a Houston multifamily loan that transferred despite reporting 93% occupancy and above breakeven debt service coverage. And then we have one of my favorites this week, a surprise mall payoff that a lot of folks thought was going to take a loss. So we have a lot of good property type stories highlighting the through line for this week. Higher rates just make us sharp on our pencils, be a little bit more selective, but the deal volume should persist absent any major macro shocks. And that's the big question here. So let's turn back the clock to Jackson Hole last week. Warsh's central message was that the Federal Reserve's 2% inflation target is firm, inflation is still too high, and policymakers have more work that they can do unless they become confident price growth is moving toward that target at sufficient speed. So in other words, it was a hawkish tilt that was designed to say, we're prepared to do something this year, specifically at the September meeting, if nothing changes our view. He also made a broader point about Fed communications. Warsh wants to rely less heavily on forward guidance. We've talked about that and give investors fewer clues about the likely path of interest rates. But I'll be curious to see what happens with other Fed speakers. We have some big names out this week. I think even Chris Waller was on the agenda. So I'll be curious to see how much that holds for other Fed speakers or if that's primarily a Warsh rule. His argument is that markets should process the economic data independently instead of looking to the Fed for their trade. So the immediate market reaction last week was fairly dramatic. The two-year Treasury yields, which is sensitive Fed policy, jumped about 13 basis points on Friday. pending_qa.q: Which university markets show the strongest student housing operating metrics among top college football programs?
pending_qa.r: Penn State led with the strongest operating results with occupancy of 94.3% and a debt service coverage ratio of 1.94 times. BYU had the strongest median DSCR at 2.06 times, and Michigan recorded the highest occupancy among the top ten at 96%. Across all top 25 football campuses, the overall occupancy was 91.5% and median DSCR was 1.68 times.

pending_qa.q: How much revenue do leading college football programs generate annually?
pending_qa.r: University of Texas led with $298 million in total college football revenue, with total athletic revenue across all sports at $343 million. Texas A&M was second at $218 million, LSU third at $213 million, Nebraska fourth at $197 million, Georgia at $195 million, Penn State at $193 million, Alabama at $192 million, and Ohio State at $185 million.

pending_qa.q: What institutional capital movements occurred in the student housing sector recently?
pending_qa.r: Aries and Scion Group acquired a four-property, over 2,300-bed student housing portfolio for $435 million, or approximately $187,800 per bed, located near University of Georgia, University of Tennessee, and Texas State University. This was their second major acquisition of the year, following a $910 million purchase of 12 properties with over 7,500 beds from Harrison Street Asset Management in May. Scion is also separately agreeing to acquire Student Quarters for approximately $1.5 billion, adding 13,000 beds.

pending_qa.q: How are Treasury yields and Federal Reserve policy expectations shifting market sentiment?
pending_qa.r: The 10-year Treasury yield pushed to 4.8% following Kevin Warsh's Jackson Hole address, with the 30-year approaching 5.3%, representing a full-on shift across the curve. The implied probability of a quarter-point rate hike in September increased from roughly 35% before Warsh's speech to 60% by the end of the day, with markets treating the 5% threshold on the 10-year as a critical psychological pivot point for the commercial real estate landscape.

pending_qa.q: What do recent employment data indicate about labor market momentum?
pending_qa.r: ADP reported only 38,000 new private sector jobs in August, the weakest gain since January. The JOLTS report showed job openings remained relatively stable but hiring declined, reinforcing a slow hire, slow fire market dynamic. The payroll benchmark revision for August 2026 was only 79,000 jobs, compared to a 911,000 job reduction in the March 2025 estimate, confirming that employment growth was already weak before recent reports.

pending_qa.q: What concerns exist regarding U.S. debt levels and fiscal sustainability?
pending_qa.r: The U.S. national debt has reached $40 trillion, with interest payments projected to surpass defense spending. Research indicates that growth alone cannot solve the deficit problem—while AI and productivity gains will help stem the bleeding, they will not reverse course or reduce outstanding debt levels. Political action requiring reduction of entitlements and significant belt-tightening is necessary, yet there is insufficient political will to implement the deep cuts required.

pending_qa.q: How do per-unit valuations differ between student housing properties at top football schools versus academically-ranked universities?
pending_qa.r: Securitized student housing balance averaged approximately $70,000 per unit for football schools, which is nearly identical to overall student housing. However, U.S. News-ranked schools showed much higher valuations at approximately $121,000 per unit, reflecting the density and more expensive properties in high-cost markets associated with those institutions.

pending_qa.q: What demographic trends will impact student housing demand in coming years?
pending_qa.r: The 2025 cohort is the largest enrollment cohort expected for the coming years, after which birth rates drop off, creating a gradual slide in enrollment projections. This year may represent the best conditions for some schools for quite a while, though schools with strong brand identity and athletic success will likely persist and continue to perform well due to their enrollment durability and appeal to prospective students.
